blocks.text: The ethics of attribution in news

Attribution is the bedrock of credibility. When you attribute information, you tell the reader exactly where the knowledge originated. This transparency allows the public to assess the reliability of the claim. Using phrases like sources say is a standard way to signal that you have verified information through private channels. It is not just about avoiding plagiarism. It is about building a chain of custody for every fact in your story.

Attribution becomes tricky when you deal with press releases versus original interviews. Research shows that journalists are often more careful with the work of their peers than they are with corporate press materials. This inconsistency can lead to accidental recycling of language. If you copy a press release without attribution, you are essentially publishing someone else's marketing as your own reporting. This is a common trap for time-strapped reporters.

Most attribution errors are not malicious. They are the result of systemic pressure. The rise of churnalism has forced many reporters to focus on high-speed production. When you have to file three stories before lunch, your brain looks for shortcuts. You might reuse a paragraph from a previous draft or copy a quote from a wire service without properly crediting the original author. This is where the fundamental attribution error comes in. You might think a colleague is lazy, but they might just be working under impossible deadlines.

items: Constant deadline pressure reduces the time available for deep verification.
Burnout lowers your cognitive capacity to catch small errors before hitting publish.
Lack of standardized documentation makes it hard to track where facts came from.
Over-reliance on digital snippets encourages copy-paste habits over original synthesis.

blocks.text: You do not need expensive software to fix your attribution habits. Start by changing how you store your research. Never keep raw notes in your email. Move them into a structured system. If you use Google Docs, use the comment feature to link back to the source of every claim. If you use Word, use the track changes feature to keep your original notes separate from your draft copy.

items: Create a dedicated folder for each story to house all primary documents.
Use a citation manager like Zotero to track your sources as you find them.
Implement a self-check rule: every fact must have a link or a document reference.
Take five minutes at the end of each day to verify the attribution of your latest draft.

blocks.text: How Lazur helps you stay ethical

Lazur acts as a bridge between your quick notes and your final draft. When you are interviewing someone, you can hold the option key and tell Lazur to capture the main points of the conversation. Because Lazur keeps your notes on your Mac, you have a local record of what was said. This helps you avoid misquoting or misattributing claims later on.

Your Mac is a powerful tool for investigative work. Use apps like DEVONthink to create a local corpus of your research. This keeps your data off the cloud and under your control. When you are drafting, use the split-screen view in macOS. Keep your primary sources on the left and your document on the right. This visual separation makes it much easier to attribute every sentence as you write it.

faq.question: Why do journalists say sources say instead of naming them?
faq.answer: Journalists use this phrasing to protect the identity of confidential sources who might face retaliation if named. It also signals that the information is being provided by a third party rather than being directly observed by the reporter.

faq.question: Is it plagiarism to copy a press release?
faq.answer: Yes, if you present the text as your own writing. You should always attribute the information to the organization that issued the press release and use quotation marks for any direct language taken from it.

faq.question: How can I avoid attribution errors when I am in a rush?
faq.answer: Create a simple template for your notes that forces you to write the source name next to every fact. Never copy and paste text directly into your draft without adding the citation immediately.

costs.title: Loss of credibility
costs.text: A single attribution error can ruin a career and destroy public trust in your reporting.

costs.title: Legal risks
costs.text: Poor attribution can lead to claims of plagiarism or defamation, which are costly to resolve.

costs.title: Burnout
costs.text: Trying to maintain high standards under extreme speed pressure leads to exhaustion.

causes.title: Speed pressure
causes.text: The demand for constant content forces reporters to take shortcuts.

causes.title: Cognitive bias
causes.text: It is easy to misattribute information when you are tired or distracted.

causes.title: Lack of process
causes.text: Many newsrooms lack a standard way to track source documentation.

fixes.title: Use a citation manager
fixes.text: Apps like Zotero keep your sources organized and metadata intact.

fixes.title: Transparent policies
fixes.text: Always link to your original source material to show your work.

fixes.title: Structured notes
fixes.text: Pair every fact with its source immediately in your notes app.
